science.title: Barriers, motivators, and alternative safety strategies associated with firearm storage decisions among U.S. firearm owners
science.description: Firearm-related injury and suicide remain major public health concerns in the United States. Safe firearm storage is a well-established strategy for reducing risk, yet adoption varies widely across gun-owning households. This study aimed to characterize firearm storage behaviors, openness to alternative safety measures, and key motivators for behavioral change among a national sample of firearm owners. Data were drawn from a national cross-sectional survey of adults in the United States who reported owning or having access to a firearm. Participants were recruited using stratified national sampling to ensure demographic and geographic representation. Survey weights provided by the panel vendor were applied to all analyses to approximate population-level estimates. Weighted means and proportions were calculated for descriptive analyses. Associations between demographic characteristics and the use of gun cases, safes, or lockboxes were evaluated using survey-weighted generalized linear models. Among firearm-owning respondents, 59.1% reported using a gun case, safe, or lockbox. Safe storage was more common in households with children and increased with carrying frequency, but it declined among those who reported carrying a firearm daily. Individuals who did not use traditional locking devices frequently relied on alternative practices such as keeping firearms unloaded or storing ammunition separately. Participants also reported moderate willingness to adopt additional safety measures, including motion alarms and cable locks. 52.5% of respondents indicated that they intend to keep at least one firearm unlocked regardless of life circumstances. Among respondents willing to change their storage practices, top-two-box endorsement was highest for child presence (97.3%) and household mental or physical health concerns (97.2%). Firearm owners engage in a wide range of storage practices, including both traditional locking methods and alternative safety strategies. Motivators related to child safety and household health concerns appear especially influential and may serve as effective focal points for intervention. The findings underscore the need for flexible, personalized approaches to lethal means safety that reflect real-world behaviors and concerns among gun owners.

science.title: Sexual dimorphism in fetal brain gene co-expression networks as a possible etiological factor of sex-biased autism prevalence
science.description: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) affects more males than females in an approximate ratio of 4:1, yet the biological bases of this imbalance remain unclear. Here, we explored the hypothesis that part of the male-biased vulnerability could arise from sex-specific baseline organization of gene regulatory networks during fetal brain development. To test this, we analyzed post-mortem cortical samples spanning a critical spatiotemporal window implicated in ASD pathophysiology and built sex-specific and consensus co-expression networks using weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA). Four modules were enriched for ASD-associated genes: two related to transcriptional regulation and two associated with neurodevelopment and synaptic function. Despite an overall conserved modular constitution between males and females, sex-dependent differences in levels of expression, module topology and inter-modular coordination were observed. Interestingly, the distribution of rare de novo variants found in mutation-intolerant genes in ASD individuals diverged across modules between males and females. Altogether, our results indicate that male and female fetal brains share core ASD-related molecular programs, but differ in their structural organization. These sex-specific regulatory contexts likely modulate the functional impact of ASD-risk variants and contribute to the marked sex bias in ASD susceptibility.
